newsitem.title: INDIA: India state keeps vigil after leader's arrest.
newsitem.headline: India state keeps vigil after leader's arrest.

text.p: Authorities in India's second most populous state prepared for trouble on Thursday after the arrest of a charismatic politician in a corruption scandal.

Former Bihar state chief minister Laloo Prasad Yadav surrendered before a special court on Wednesday and has been ordered held in judicial custody for two weeks while investigators question him in connection with a $280 million farm funds scandal.
Politicians and officials said they saw no immediate threat of violence although supporters of Yadav, a low-caste leader, blocked roads on Wednesday and called a general strike for Friday.
"There will be no looting or violence. All business will be closed, that's all," said a police official, who did not want to be identified. "It is in their (ruling party's) interest."
The state capital, Patna, was quiet on Thursday, patrolled by more than 500 paramilitary police reinforcements.
Soldiers in blue fatigues camped near fortified vans equipped with anti-riot gear at key points in the city, which has a population of one million.

Yadav's supporters said they would offer themselves for arrest for five days from Saturday under a "jail bharo" (fill the jails) protest against his arrest. Yadav says he is innocent in the scandal, which involves the alleged embezzlement of state animal welfare funds.
"We will offer ourselves collectively for arrest," said activist Vishwanath Kesri.
Yadav's wife, Rabri Devi, an unschooled housewife who was catapulted into the chief minister's job last Friday when he resigned under pressure, appealed for calm.

"Keeping in view the political and social challenges facing us, it is imperative that we do not let the situation in the state worsen in any way..." Devi said in a front-page advertisement in leading local dailies.

Bihar is one of India's poorest states and is frequently wracked by violence between lower and upper Hindu castes. Landowners maintain private armies in the resource-rich region where poor roads and communications make lawkeeping difficult.

Yadav's restive supporters said they were keen to help his wife, who was rubber-stamped by lawmakers from Yadav's Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) party, and responded by naming more than half the lawmakers to a record-breaking 75-member cabinet.

"This is our government, so workers will not indulge in violence even though there is great resentment among them," said acting RJD president Ranjan Yadav. "Even if the opposition provokes us, we will be quiet," another worker said.
Politicians say peace in the state is crucial for Devi because the federal government could be under pressure to dismiss her administration if law and order break down.
Yadav headed Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's Janata Dal party until July 5, when he resigned in a leadership dispute to set up the breakaway RJD group.

India's ruling 15-party United Front coalition has been sharply divided by a debate over corruption and Gujral's failure to take firm action against Yadav, who was first indicted in the farm scandal in April.

The charismatic Yadav, who ruled Bihar for seven years, travelled in a motorcade to court on Wednesday after the Supreme Court rejected his appeal for "anticipatory bail", allowed under Indian law to persons who fear arrest.
